# Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks

Haoyu Liu Affiliation: UC Berkeley, IEOR & BAIR Affiliation: Google
Affiliation:  Work done during an internship at Google.    Dingcheng Li
Affiliation: Google Deepmind haoyuliu@berkeley.edu, {dingchengli,
lukasr}@google.com, zyzheng@berkeley.edu    Lukas Rutishauser
Affiliation: Google    Zeyu Zheng Affiliation: UC Berkeley, IEOR & BAIR

###### Abstract

Multimodal web agents that process both screenshots and accessibility
trees are increasingly deployed to interact with web interfaces, yet
their dual-stream architecture opens an underexplored attack surface: an
adversary who injects content into the webpage DOM simultaneously
corrupts _both_ observation channels with a consistent deceptive
narrative. Our vulnerability analysis on MiniWob++ reveals that attacks
including a visual component far outperform text-only injections,
exposing critical gaps in text-centric VLM safety training. Motivated by
this finding, we propose Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety
Training (DMAST), a framework that formalizes the agent–attacker
interaction as a two-player zero-sum Markov game and co-trains both
players through a three-stage pipeline: (1) imitation learning from a
strong teacher model, (2) oracle-guided supervised fine-tuning that uses
a novel _zero-acknowledgment_ strategy to instill task-focused reasoning
under adversarial noise, and (3) adversarial reinforcement learning via
Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) self-play. On
out-of-distribution tasks, DMAST substantially mitigates adversarial
risks while simultaneously doubling task completion efficiency. Our
approach significantly outperforms established training-based and
prompt-based defenses, demonstrating genuine co-evolutionary progress
and robust generalization to complex, unseen environments.

Figure 1: Overview of the agent–attacker interaction process. At each
timestep, the attacker observes the clean webpage state and injects
malicious HTML/CSS into the DOM, simultaneously corrupting both the
screenshot and the accessibility tree. The agent then acts on the
modified observations, and the environment transitions accordingly.

## 1 Introduction

Web agents powered by Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly
deployed to autonomously navigate and interact with web interfaces on
behalf of users. Modern agents ingest both a rendered screenshot and a
structured accessibility tree (AXTree) extracted from the DOM,
leveraging complementary strengths: the screenshot captures rich visual
context, while the accessibility tree provides precise labels and types
of interactive elements. This dual-stream architecture has driven steady
progress on web interaction benchmarks ([Liu et al., 2018](#bib.bib25);
[Koh et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)), yet it also opens an underexplored
attack surface. An adversary who injects content into the webpage’s DOM
simultaneously corrupts _both_ channels, presenting the agent with a
consistent deceptive narrative that is far harder to detect than a
single-modality perturbation.

Despite growing concerns about agent security ([Greshake et al.,
2023](#bib.bib13); [Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)), most existing work
studies text-based prompt injections and image-based attacks in
isolation, leaving a critical gap: how vulnerable are multimodal web
agents when attackers coordinate across modalities? We address this
question with a systematic vulnerability analysis on the MiniWob++
benchmark using a state-of-the-art instruction-tuned VLM. The results
reveal that attacks including a visual component (either image-only
(34.4% attacker success) or coordinated dual-modality (35.7%)) are much
more effective at inducing safety jailbreaks than text-only injections
(24.1%). This disparity aligns with recent findings that image-based
injections often bypass text-centric safety filters ([Yeo and Choi,
2025](#bib.bib9)), and it demonstrates that current VLMs are not
equipped to handle visual deceptions such as typographic overlays, fake
system dialogs, or phishing forms embedded in screenshots.

Motivated by these findings, we propose Dual-Modality Multi-Stage
Adversarial Safety Training (DMAST), a framework for hardening
multimodal web agents through adversarial co-evolution. We formalize the
agent–attacker interaction as a two-player zero-sum Markov game and
design a unified HTML injection mechanism where the attacker generates
structured DOM modifications executed in the browser runtime. Since both
the screenshot and accessibility tree are rendered from the same DOM, a
single injection automatically and consistently alters both modalities,
closely modeling real-world threats. Both the agent and attacker are
instantiated from the same VLM with shared weights, enabling efficient
co-evolution: as the model learns to craft attacks, it simultaneously
develops awareness of those patterns, which transfers to defense.

Training proceeds through a three-stage pipeline. _Stage 1 (Imitation
Learning)_ distills expert trajectories from a stronger teacher model
into a smaller student model, providing a stable initialization for both
roles. _Stage 2 (Oracle-Guided SFT)_ augments the training data with a
novel denoising strategy: an oracle with privileged access to both clean
and attacked views generates task-focused Chain-of-Thought reasoning
that teaches the student to maintain goal-directed behavior amid
adversarial noise, without ever acknowledging the attack. _Stage 3
(Adversarial RL)_ co-evolves the agent and attacker through self-play
using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), driving both players
toward increasingly sophisticated strategies.

Experiments on held-out MiniWob++ tasks and out-of-distribution
VisualWebArena tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of DMAST. On our
curated VisualWebArena tasks with adversarial setup, the full pipeline
reduces attacker success from 41.2% (base model) to 21.4% while
improving agent task completion from 6.2% to 10.2%, outperforming
baselines including SPAG ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)), Automatic
Red Teaming ([Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Samvelyan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)), Online SFT ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib29)),
and pure prompt-based defenses. Each training stage provides cumulative
improvements, with oracle-guided SFT instilling structural priors that
persist through RL, and cross-checkpoint evaluation confirms that both
agent and attacker capabilities genuinely co-evolve through self-play.

## 2 Related Work

##### Safety of LLM-Based Web Agents.

Indirect prompt injection attacks can compromise LLM-integrated
applications by embedding malicious instructions in external
data ([Greshake et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)). In the web agent context,
AdvWeb ([Xu et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)) injects adversarial prompts into
HTML fields invisible to the rendered page. Benchmarks such as
AgentDojo ([Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)) and
MultiTrust ([Zhang et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)) consistently reveal that
current agents remain vulnerable to diverse safety attacks.

##### Attacks on Multimodal Models.

The integration of visual encoders into LLMs expands the attack surface.
Typographic attacks ([Wang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib3); [Qraitem et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Chung et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)) superimpose
misleading text onto images, while adversarial perturbations ([Shayegani
et al., 2023](#bib.bib6); [Aichberger et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)) add
imperceptible noise to fool image encoders. Beyond single-modality
attacks, cross-modal injections ([Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib7))
simultaneously corrupt both visual and textual channels, exploiting the
fusion process to hijack agent decision-making process and execute
unauthorized tasks. [Yeo and Choi (2025)](#bib.bib9) systematically
evaluated eight modern multimodal models and found that image-based
injections were among the most effective attack types, often bypassing
text-only content filters.

##### Adversarial Training and Self-Play.

Adversarial reinforcement learning, where an agent co-evolves against a
learned adversary, has proven effective in various domains including
strategic games ([Silver et al., 2017](#bib.bib19); [Vinyals et al.,
2019](#bib.bib18)), dynamic control ([Wurman et al., 2022](#bib.bib20)),
and security ([Cui et al., 2023](#bib.bib22)). For LLMs, self-play has
been applied to instruction following ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib21))
and preference alignment ([Wu et al., 2024](#bib.bib23)). In multimodal
safety, [Rashid and Rivas (2024)](#bib.bib14) and [Schlarmann et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib15) used adversarial fine-tuning for robust vision
encoders, and ProEAT ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib16)) proposed a
two-stage adversarial framework for jailbreak defense across modalities.
Our work extends this paradigm to web agents facing coordinated
multimodal attacks.

## 3 Problem Formulation

In this section, we formalize the multimodal web agent setting as a
two-player game, describe our HTML-based injection mechanism, and
present empirical evidence demonstrating the increased vulnerability of
multimodal agents under visual attacks, justifying the need for our
multimodal adversarial training framework. We focus on sensitive data
leakage as the primary threat: the attacker aims to trick the agent into
revealing private information (e.g., passwords) through crafted
injections into the agent’s observations.

### 3.1 Problem Setup

Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
illustrates the interaction process between the agent, attacker, and
environment. We formulate the adversarial interaction as a two-player
zero-sum Markov game
$`\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A}_{\text{agt}},\mathcal{A}_{\text{atk}},\mathcal{P},R\rangle`$,
where $`\mathcal{S}`$ is the state space (webpage states),
$`\mathcal{A}_{\text{agt}}`$ and $`\mathcal{A}_{\text{atk}}`$ are the
action spaces of the agent and attacker, $`\mathcal{P}`$ is the
transition function governed by the browser, and $`R`$ is the reward.

##### Agent.

The agent receives a task description $`G`$ and synthetic user data
$`U`$. The agent’s goal is to complete the task while avoiding leaking
the sensitive information. At each timestep $`t`$, it observes a
(possibly modified) screenshot $`I_{t}`$ and accessibility tree
$`T_{t}`$. Its policy
$`\pi_{\theta}^{\text{agt}}\!:\mathcal{I}\!\times\!\mathcal{T}\!\times\!\mathcal{G}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{A}_{\text{agt}}`$
generates browser actions (click, type, scroll). This dual-modality
design is essential for web agents: the screenshot provides rich visual
information necessary for decision-making, and the text modality
supplies accurate labels for precise execution. However, as we
demonstrate below, the reliance on both modalities introduces a new
attack surface. Agents face a significantly harder detection problem
when injections appear on the visual contents.

##### Attacker.

We model an adversary whose goal is to induce the agent into revealing
the sensitive user information $`U`$. At each timestep $`t`$, the
attacker observes the _clean_ state $`(I_{t},T_{t})`$ and task $`G`$,
but has no access to the agent’s weights, prompts, or user data $`U`$
(black-box setting). Its policy $`\pi_{\phi}^{\text{atk}}`$ generates an
injection action $`\alpha_{t}`$ that modifies the agent’s observations
to produce $`(I^{\prime}_{t},T^{\prime}_{t})`$.

##### Interaction and Rewards.

At each timestep, the attacker first observes the clean state
$`(I_{t},T_{t})`$ and generates attack
$`\alpha_{t}\sim\pi_{\phi}^{\text{atk}}(I_{t},T_{t},G)`$, producing
modified observations $`(I^{\prime}_{t},T^{\prime}_{t})`$; the agent
then selects action
$`a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}^{\text{agent}}(I^{\prime}_{t},T^{\prime}_{t},G)`$
based on these modified observations; the environment then transitions
to $`s_{t+1}\sim\mathcal{P}(\cdot|s_{t},a_{t})`$. The episode ends when
the task is completed, user data is revealed, or the step limit is
reached. The reward structure incentivizes both task completion and
security. Specifically: (1) Task completed, data safe:
$`R_{\text{agt}}=+1`$, $`R_{\text{atk}}=-1`$; (2) Task failed, data
safe: $`R_{\text{agt}}=-1`$, $`R_{\text{atk}}=-1`$; (3) User data
revealed: $`R_{\text{agt}}=-1`$, $`R_{\text{atk}}=+1`$. Notably, when
the task fails without data leakage, both parties are penalized. This
incentivizes the agent to complete the task (not merely refuse to act).
The reward will be used as the reward signal for the reinforcement
learning training process introduced in
Section [4](#S4 "4 Methodology ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks").

#### 3.1.1 HTML-Based Injection Mechanism

We implement a unified HTML injection mechanism: the attacker generates
structured HTML/CSS code injected into the live webpage DOM via
JavaScript execution. This design achieves (1) _cross-modal
consistency_: the screenshot and accessibility tree always agree, (2)
_computational efficiency_: requiring only JavaScript execution rather
than GPU-based image generation, and (3) _semantic richness_: the
attacker can create interactive elements (forms, buttons) that appear in
the accessibility tree with proper labels, indistinguishable from
legitimate elements.

Concretely, the attacker’s action
$`\alpha_{t}=(\texttt{target},\texttt{position},\texttt{html},\texttt{css})`$
consists of a CSS selector specifying the target injection point, a
positional directive (prepend/append/before/after), an HTML payload, and
optional CSS styling. This tuple is compiled into JavaScript, executed
in the browser, and all injected elements are tagged for clean rollback
between steps (details in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A HTML Injection Execution Details ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")).
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1.1 HTML-Based Injection Mechanism ‣ 3.1 Problem Setup ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
illustrates the mechanism on a MiniWob++ date-selection task.
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Trajectory Examples ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
provides full trajectory examples illustrating both attacker-successful
and agent-successful interactions.

### 3.2 Vulnerability Analysis

We now investigate how attack modality influences agent vulnerability.
Recent evidence ([Yeo and Choi, 2025](#bib.bib9)) suggests that models
trained predominantly on text fail to neutralize malicious instructions
in visual channels. To validate this hypothesis, we conduct a systematic
vulnerability assessment using the framework defined above.

We instantiate both agent and attacker as Gemma-3-27B-IT ([Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24)) and evaluate on MiniWob++ tasks ([Liu et al.,
2018](#bib.bib25)). MiniWob++ comprises a diverse suite of HTML-based
interactive tasks ranging from simple UI manipulation to complex
multi-step reasoning. Since MiniWob++ tasks are not originally designed
to include sensitive data for defensive evaluation, following [Wang et
al. (2025c)](#bib.bib1), we augment prompts with synthetic user data and
detect leakage via string matching. We evaluate the model on 125
distinct tasks, collecting 8 episodes per task (totaling 1,000 episodes
per configuration) across four experimental conditions: (1) No Attack,
in which agent receives clean observations;(2) Text-Only Attack, in
which agent receives clean screenshot but attacked accessibility
tree;(3) Image-Only Attack, in which agent receives attacked screenshot
but clean accessibility tree; and (4) Dual Attack, in which agent
receives attacked screenshot and attacked accessibility tree.

Crucially, the attacker pipeline is identical across all conditions. It
always generates a full HTML injection, and conditions differ only in
what is delivered to the agent, isolating the modality effect. We report
Agent Success Rate (Agt $`\uparrow`$, task completed safely) and
Attacker Success Rate (Atk $`\downarrow`$, data leaked) among those
tasks.

| Config.    | Agent          | Attacker       |
| ---------- | -------------- | -------------- |
| No Attack  | 36.9$`\pm`$1.5 | N/A            |
| Text-Only  | 15.9$`\pm`$1.2 | 24.1$`\pm`$1.4 |
| Image-Only | 15.6$`\pm`$1.2 | 34.4$`\pm`$1.5 |
| Dual       | 15.8$`\pm`$1.2 | 35.7$`\pm`$1.5 |

Table 1: Vulnerability analysis across attack modalities (%, MiniWob++,
Gemma-3-27B-IT, 1,000 episodes) showing agent success rate and attacker
success rate with standard errors.

As shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.2 Vulnerability Analysis ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks"),
all injection modalities reduce agent success from 36.9% to
$`\sim`$15.6–15.9%. More critically, attacker success rates differ
sharply: Image-Only achieves 34.4%, far exceeding Text-Only at 24.1%,
while Dual attacks reach 35.7%. This pattern aligns with prior
findings ([Yeo and Choi, 2025](#bib.bib9)) and suggests that current VLM
safety training, which is predominantly text-centric, fails to cover
visual deceptions such as typographic overlays. These findings motivate
the design of a training framework that explicitly exposes agents to
multimodal adversarial attacks. In the next section, we present DMAST, a
three-stage adversarial training pipeline built upon the Markov game
formulation and HTML injection mechanism introduced above.

## 4 Methodology

Building on the formulation in
Section [3](#S3 "3 Problem Formulation ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks"),
we present Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training
(DMAST), our framework for training robust multimodal web agents through
co-evolution of agent and attacker policies via a three-stage training
pipeline. The procedure is summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks").

1: Policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$, Teacher $`\pi_{\text{tch}}`$, Oracle
$`\pi_{\text{orc}}`$, Tasks $`\mathcal{G}`$

2:  

3: Stage 1: Imitation Learning.

4: Collect clean & adversarial demos via $`\pi_{\text{tch}}`$; SFT
$`\pi_{\theta}`$.

5:

6: Stage 2: Oracle-Guided SFT.

7: $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{den}}\!\leftarrow\!\emptyset`$;  collect clean
trajectories $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{cl}}`$ via $`\pi_{\text{teach}}`$.

8: for each step $`(o_{t},c_{t},a_{t})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{cl}}`$ do

9:   $`\alpha_{t}\!\sim\!\pi_{\text{tch}}^{\text{atk}}(o_{t})`$; 
$`o^{\prime}_{t}\!\leftarrow\!\text{Env}(o_{t},\alpha_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Inject attack

10:
  $`c_{t}^{\text{aug}}\!\leftarrow\!\pi_{\text{orc}}(o^{\prime}_{t},o_{t},G)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Task-focused CoT

11:

12: end for

13: SFT $`\pi_{\theta}`$ on
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{den}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{cl}}`$.

16: for iteration $`k=1,\dots,K`$ do

17:   for episode $`e=1,\dots,M`$ do

18:    Sample $`G\!\sim\!\mathcal{G}`$; observe $`o_{1}`$

19:    for $`t=1,\dots,T`$ do

20:      $`\alpha_{t}\!\sim\!\pi_{\theta}^{\text{atk}}(o_{t},G)`$
$`\triangleright`$ Attack

21:      $`o^{\prime}_{t}\!\leftarrow\!\text{Env}(o_{t},\alpha_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Inject

Algorithm 1 DMAST: Training Procedure

Both the agent and attacker are instantiated from the _same_ VLM with
shared weights, differentiated only by role-specific system prompts.
This halves the memory footprint and enables emergent co-evolution.
Although DMAST is model-agnostic, we adopt a teacher–student paradigm: a
larger, more capable _teacher_ model generates high-quality trajectories
for data collection, while a smaller _student_ model serves as the
target policy for iterative self-play training, which would be
computationally prohibitive with the teacher. We would first train the
student model on the trajectories generated by the teacher model to
improve its initial capabilities, as described in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Stage 1: Imitation Learning ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks").

### 4.1 Stage 1: Imitation Learning

Direct adversarial self-play often suffers from cold-start dynamics when
the initial policy lacks the specialized strategic depth required for
exploring meaningful interactions ([Vinyals et al., 2019](#bib.bib18);
[Silver et al., 2017](#bib.bib19)). To provide stable initialization, we
begin with imitation learning to distill the abilities embedded in
expert trajectories from the teacher model. We collect two categories of
trajectories using the teacher: _adversarial episodes_ (agent completes
tasks in adversarial settings with attackers) and _clean episodes_
(agent completes tasks without attacks). Including clean episodes
prevents the student from becoming overly defensive. From these, we
curate agent trajectories $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{agent}}`$ (successful
completions from both settings) and attacker trajectories
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{attacker}}`$ (successful attacks). Following [Wang
et al. (2025c)](#bib.bib1), we fine-tune the student with a
KL-regularized SFT objective using LoRA ([Hu et al., 2022](#bib.bib2)):

|     |                                               |                                                                                              |             |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}^{r}`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{r}}\!\left[\log\pi\_{\theta}(y            | x)\right]`$ |     |     |
|     |                                               | $`\displaystyle\quad+\beta_{\text{SFT}}\cdot D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})`$ |             | (1) |

where $`r\in\{\text{agent},\text{attacker}\}`$ denotes the role,
$`\mathcal{D}_{r}`$ is the corresponding trajectory set, where
$`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$ is the reference policy (the original pretrained
model), and $`\beta_{\text{SFT}}`$ is the KL regularization coefficient
that prevents the model from deviating too far from its original
capabilities.

### 4.2 Stage 2: Oracle-Guided SFT

While imitation learning establishes a behavioral baseline, the
resulting policy often lacks the resilience to maintain goal-directed
behavior under adversarial perturbations. To bridge this gap, we
introduce an oracle-guided data augmentation stage designed to instill a
strong prior of _task-focused mission adherence_ before the agent enters
the RL loop. As demonstrated in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Experiments ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks"),
this stage yields the most pronounced gains in agent task completion
rate, confirming its effectiveness in strengthening functional utility
under adversarial conditions.

The pipeline operates in four steps to construct a synthetic “denoising”
dataset:

1.  1.  First, we collect _golden trajectories_, which are successful task
        completions by the teacher agent on clean (unattacked) observations
        $`o_{t}=(I_{t},T_{t},G)`$. The agent’s response is represented as
        $`(c_{t},a_{t})`$, where $`c_{t}`$ is the Chain-of-Thought (CoT)
        reasoning trace and $`a_{t}`$ is the action taken by the agent.
2.  2.  Second, for each step in a golden trajectory, the teacher attacker
        synthesizes a multimodal injection attack on the clean observation
        and generate the corresponding attacked observation
        $`o^{\prime}_{t}=(I^{\prime}_{t},T^{\prime}_{t},G)`$. This produces
        a pair of observations, one clean and one attacked, that share the
        exact same target action.
3.  3.  Third, we employ an _oracle_ model to generate a _task-focused_
        Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning trace. Leveraging its privileged
        access to both the clean and attacked views, the oracle identifies
        the correct task elements but generates a reasoning path that is
        strictly constrained to exclusively ground its reasoning in
        task-relevant elements without mentioning the attack (see
        Appendix [D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Oracle Prompt for Task-Focused CoT Generation ‣ Appendix D Prompts ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
        for the detailed prompt used for oracle model). The oracle-generated
        CoT, denoted as $`c_{t}^{\text{aug}}`$, replaces the original
        reasoning trace $`c_{t}`$ to form a new synthetic training sample
        $`(o^{\prime}_{t},c_{t}^{\text{aug}},a_{t})`$. Crucially, while the
        observation changes from $`o_{t}`$ to $`o^{\prime}_{t}`$ and the
        reasoning changes from $`c_{t}`$ to $`c_{t}^{\text{aug}}`$, the
        target action $`a_{t}`$ remains invariant, enforcing the constraint
        that the attack should not alter the agent’s decision.
4.  4.  Finally, the augmented data
        $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{aug}}=\{(o^{\prime}_{t},c_{t}^{\text{aug}},a_{t})\}`$
        is mixed with the golden trajectories
        $`\mathcal{D}_{\text{clean}}`$.

After collecting the oracle-guided data, we fine-tune the student model
using the same SFT objective as in Stage 1.

### 4.3 Stage 3: Adversarial RL (Self-Play)

After supervised learning, we employ reinforcement learning to enable
the agent and attacker to co-evolve through adversarial self-play within
the Markov game defined in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Problem Setup ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks").

We use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib26)) as our RL algorithm. Unlike traditional policy
gradient methods that require training a separate value network to
estimate advantages, GRPO computes advantages by comparing sampled
responses within a group. In the training loop, we update the agent and
attacker using the collected multi-turn trajectories. For each task, we
sample a group of $`N`$ full episodes and calculate group-relative
advantages for each action step. For example, the advantage for all the
tokens in the $`t`$-th step in episode $`n`$ is:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \hat{A}_{t}^{n}=\frac{r_{T}^{n}-\bar{r}}{\sigma_{r}+\epsilon},
       ```                                                             |     | (2) |

where $`\bar{r}`$ and $`\sigma_{r}`$ are the mean and standard deviation
of $`\{r_{T}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}`$, and $`\epsilon`$ is a small constant for
stability. We omit role subscripts for brevity, as both agent and
attacker share the same advantage computation. The policy is updated via
a clipped surrogate objective:

|     |     |                                                                                                                                                                     |     |     |
| --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}=\mathbb{E}\Bigg[\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{n,t,j}\bigg(\min\!\big(\rho_{t,j}^{n}\hat{A}_{t}^{n},\;`$                                               |     |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\quad\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{t,j}^{n},1\!-\!\epsilon_{l},1\!+\!\epsilon_{h})\hat{A}_{t}^{n}\big)\!-\!\beta_{\text{RL}}D_{\text{KL}}\bigg)\Bigg],`$ |     | (3) |

where
$`\rho_{t,j}^{n}=\pi(a_{t,j}^{n}|o_{t}^{n},a_{t,<j}^{n})/\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot)`$
is the importance sampling ratio, $`Z`$ is a normalizing constant,
$`\epsilon_{l}`$ and $`\epsilon_{h}`$ are clipping thresholds, and
$`\beta_{\text{RL}}`$ controls the KL penalty toward the SFT checkpoint
to prevent catastrophic forgetting.

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
summarizes our complete training procedure. The shared-weight design
enables efficient training while the role-specific prompting allows
specialization of agent and attacker behaviors.

## 5 Experiments

In this section, we systematically evaluate DMAST to assess its efficacy
in fortifying web agents against adversarial manipulations. Our
experiments are designed to investigate: (i) the comparative performance
against other defense methods; (ii) the co-evolutionary dynamics between
the agent and the attacker during self-play, and (iii) the marginal
contribution of each training stage.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

##### Models.

We instantiate our framework using Gemma-3-12B-IT as the student agent
and Gemma-3-27B-IT as the teacher model for trajectory synthesis. During
the evaluation phase, the 27B model serves as a fixed, high-capacity
adversary to provide a rigorous and consistent benchmark for defense
performance.

##### Training Data Synthesis.

All training phases are conducted using the tasks in the MiniWob++
benchmark ([Liu et al., 2018](#bib.bib25)), excluding a fixed set of 28
tasks reserved for evaluation. Similar with
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Vulnerability Analysis ‣ 3 Problem Formulation ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks"),we
augment the agent’s prompt with synthetic sensitive information (e.g.,
passwords) and define information leakage via string-matching heuristics
on generated tool parameters.

For supervised initialization (Imitation Learning and Oracle-Guided
SFT), we utilize the full training task set. For the RL phase, we select
only tasks where both the agent and attacker exhibit non-trivial success
rates (agent $`>0.2`$ in benign settings; attacker $`>0.1`$ in
adversarial settings), ensuring a dense optimization signal for stable
co-evolutionary learning.

##### Baselines.

We benchmark DMAST against the following representative defense
paradigms, ranging from pure prompt-based defenses to RL-based defenses:
(1) SPAG ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)), which is a self-play RL
framework with an alternative optimization objective; (2) Automatic Red
Teaming (ART) ([Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib27); [Samvelyan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28)), which is a training paradigm where the agent is
optimized via RL against a fixed, automated red-teaming suite; (3)
Online SFT ([Zelikman et al., 2022](#bib.bib29)), which is an iterative
supervised fine-tuning approach that trains the agent on its successful
(safe and task-complete) trajectories; (4) Pure Prompt Defense, which is
a zero-shot strategy that relies exclusively on hand-engineered,
security-focused system prompts; and (5) Base Model, the vanilla
Gemma-3-12B-IT model without any training.

##### Evaluation Benchmarks.

To rigorously assess the defense’s robustness and generalizability, we
evaluate the models on two distinct task sets: (1) Unseen Miniwob++
Tasks: We reserve a held-out set of tasks from MiniWob++ that were
entirely excluded from the training phase. (2) Curated VisualWebArena
Tasks: We leverage VisualWebArena ([Koh et al., 2024](#bib.bib17)) to
perform evaluation on more complex, real-world web scenarios to evaluate
the model’s ability to handle out of distribution (OOD) task patterns.
We curate 100 tasks, augmenting each with synthetic sensitive user
information. An adversarial attacker is deployed to manipulate web
content to induce information leakage, providing a high-fidelity test of
the agent’s resilience.

##### Metrics.

We report two primary metrics: Task Success Rate (TSR $`\uparrow`$): The
ratio of episodes where the agent successfully completes the task
without any security breaches. Attack Success Rate (ASR $`\downarrow`$):
The frequency with which the agent inadvertently reveals sensitive
information. A superior defense is characterized by the simultaneous
maximization of TSR and minimization of ASR.

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
compares defense methods across both evaluation benchmarks. Among
training-based methods, DMAST consistently achieves the best
safety–utility trade-off. Other training-based baselines such as SPAG
and Online SFT show limited safety improvements on VisualWebArena,
failing to generalize to sophisticated cross-modal attacks, while ART
provides moderate gains but is consistently outperformed by DMAST.

Notably, Pure Prompt Defense achieves even lower ASR than all
training-based methods. However, this comes at a cost: on
VisualWebArena, TSR drops to just 3.1%, indicating that the overly
conservative prompting leads to “refusal collapse” where the agent
avoids acting altogether. Motivated by this observation, we further
evaluate the combination of DMAST with prompt-based defense. DMAST +
Prompt Defense yields the lowest ASR across both benchmarks (even
surpassing standalone Prompt Defense) while maintaining high TSR. This
confirms that the two approaches are complementary: our method equips
the agent with robust behavioral priors that prevent refusal collapse,
while safety prompts provide an additional layer of protection.

### 5.3 Analysis and Ablation Studies

##### Adversarial Co-evolutionary Dynamics.

We conduct cross-evaluation between agent and attacker checkpoints
across training iterations
(Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Adversarial Co-evolutionary Dynamics. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")).
The heatmaps reveal a classic adversarial arms race: the Iter 10 agent
improves its success rate against a base attacker from 19.6% to 31.2%
while reducing attacker success rate (7.1% $`\rightarrow`$ 4.9%).
Simultaneously, the Iter 5 attacker triples the base attacker’s success
rate, and the Iter 10 attacker specializes in bypassing trained defenses
rather than exploiting the base model, confirming genuine capability
co-evolution.

Figure 3: Cross-evaluation heatmaps of agent and attacker checkpoints

when pairing a specific agent checkpoint (column) against a specific

##### Stage-wise Contributions.

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
shows monotonic improvement through the pipeline on both benchmarks,
with each stage playing a distinct and complementary role. Across both
MiniWob++ and VisualWebArena, imitation learning primarily enhances
safety (reducing ASR), while Oracle-Guided SFT primarily boosts
functional utility (increasing TSR). Finally, RL self-play yields the
largest combined gain on both dimensions, simultaneously driving ASR to
its lowest and TSR to its highest. To further verify the necessity of
Oracle-Guided SFT, we compare the full pipeline against an ablated
variant (Imitation $`\rightarrow`$ RL) in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Stage-wise Contributions. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks").
The full pipeline consistently dominates at every RL iteration,
confirming that Oracle-Guided SFT instills robust behavioral priors that
RL optimizes rather than replaces.

##### Emergent Diversity of Attack Patterns.

We assess whether the attacker generates increasingly diverse HTML
injections over self-play RL using two complementary metrics: (1)
Distinct-$`n`$ [Li et al. (2016)](#bib.bib30), which computes the ratio
of unique $`n`$-grams to total $`n`$-grams across all generated attacks
within each iteration (higher indicates greater lexical diversity); and
(2) Self-BLEU [Zhu et al. (2018)](#bib.bib31), which measures the
average BLEU score [Papineni et al. (2002)](#bib.bib32) of each
generated attack against all other attacks in the same iteration (lower
indicates less repetition and thus higher diversity).

As shown in
Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Emergent Diversity of Attack Patterns. ‣ 5.3 Analysis and Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks"),
Distinct-$`n`$ increases and Self-BLEU decreases consistently across RL
iterations, confirming that co-evolution naturally incentivizes attack
diversification: as the agent becomes robust to previously seen
patterns, the attacker must explore novel injection strategies.
Qualitatively, pre-RL attacks are largely template-like credential forms
(e.g., generic “System Verification Required” prompts), whereas post-RL
attacks exhibit task-context awareness, and sometimes exhibit multi-step
temporal coordination, in which consecutive injections first override
the agent’s instructions and then exploit the confusion to induce data
leakage.
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Additional Attack Diversity Analysis ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
provides additional quantitative analyses (n-gram entropy, strategy
classification) as well as concrete before-and-after examples
illustrating these evolving attack patterns.

(a) Distinct-$`n`$ scores ($`\uparrow`$ indicates higher diversity).

(b) Self-BLEU scores ($`\downarrow`$ indicates higher diversity).

Figure 4: Diversity of attacker-generated HTML injections across
self-play iterations. (a) Distinct-$`n`$ measures lexical diversity
(unique $`n`$-grams / total $`n`$-grams); consistent growth indicates
increasingly varied attack text. (b) Self-BLEU measures $`n`$-gram
overlap between samples; decreasing scores confirm attacks become less
repetitive over training.

## 6 Conclusion

We presented DMAST, a framework for hardening multimodal web agents
against coordinated attacks across visual and textual observation
channels. By formalizing the agent–attacker interaction as a zero-sum
Markov game, we first identified visual injections as a particularly
potent threat vector compared to text-only attacks. Our empirical
analysis demonstrates that each phase of the proposed training pipeline
provides synergistic gains, with the full framework consistently
outperforming existing baselines on challenging out-of-distribution
tasks. Specifically, DMAST establishes a superior balance between
adversarial robustness and functional utility, a capability further
validated by the emergence of a genuine co-evolutionary arms race during
self-play. We hope our findings provide a practical foundation for
building safer multimodal AI systems and motivate future research on
scaling these defenses to broader attack objectives.

## 7 Limitations

While DMAST establishes a robust foundation for dual-modality
multi-stage adversarial safety training in web agents, we identify
several limitations that provide fertile ground for future
investigation.

##### Scope of Adversarial Objectives.

Our current experiments primarily address sensitive data leakage via
prompt injection, a critical security bottleneck in autonomous agents.
However, the threat landscape is multifaceted, encompassing others such
as control-flow hijacking and the dissemination of misinformation. It is
important to note that because DMAST is architected as a general-purpose
Markov game, extending the defense to these alternative objectives
involves only reconfiguring the reward function $`\mathcal{R}`$ rather
than modifying the underlying training paradigm. Future work could
evaluate the performance of our method on other types of adversarial
objectives.

##### Absolute Capability of Small Models.

Although our pipeline yields substantial relative improvements, the
absolute task success rate (10.2% on VisualWebArena) remains modest,
largely due to the limited capacity of the 12B student model chosen for
computational tractability. Applying DMAST to larger VLMs with stronger
base capabilities is an important direction for future work.

##### Potential Risks and Misuse

Like other adversarial robustness research, our framework studies attack
strategies in order to improve defenses. While such techniques could
potentially be misused to design more effective attacks, we believe that
the paper does not introduce new real-world attack tools or deployment
systems, and the primary benefit of this work is enabling safer
deployment of multimodal web agents by improving their robustness
against cross-modal prompt injection.

## Appendix A HTML Injection Execution Details

Concretely, the attacker’s action $`\alpha_{t}`$ consists of a
structured tuple:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\alpha_{t}=(\texttt{target},\texttt{position},\texttt{html},\texttt{css})
``` |  | (4) |

where:

- •
  target $`\in\mathcal{C}`$: a CSS selector specifying the injection
  point in the DOM (e.g., \#area for the task area, body for the full
  page).
- •
  position $`\in\{`$prepend, append, before, after$`\}`$: where to
  insert content relative to the target.
- •
  html $`\in\Sigma^{*}`$: the HTML payload containing malicious elements
  such as fake popups, phishing forms, or deceptive overlays.
- •
  css $`\in\Sigma^{*}`$: optional CSS styling for precise visual control
  (positioning, z-index layering, font styling, etc.).

The structured attack action is compiled into a self-contained
JavaScript snippet and executed in the browser runtime. The script (1)
injects any attacker-specified CSS into the document head as a \<style\>
element, (2) locates the target DOM node, (3) wraps the HTML payload in
a container element, and (4) inserts it at the specified position
relative to the target. All injected elements are tagged with a
data-attacker attribute to enable clean rollback between interaction
steps. After injection, the browser re-renders the page, and both the
screenshot (captured via the headless browser) and the accessibility
tree (extracted from the updated DOM) reflect the injected content.

## Appendix B Implementation Details

### B.1 Model Configuration

##### Agent and Attacker Models.

We use Gemma-3-12B-IT as the student model for both the agent and
attacker roles in a *self-play* setting, where both roles share the same
model weights and are differentiated only by role-specific system
prompts. Gemma-3-27B-IT serves as the teacher model for trajectory
collection in Stages 1 and 2, and as a fixed attacker for evaluation.
All models are served via vLLM with the following inference
configuration:

- •
  Maximum context length: 32,768 tokens
- •
  GPU memory utilization: 0.8
- •
  Precision: bfloat16
- •
  Maximum new tokens per generation: 4,096

For data collection during RL training, we use temperature $`=1.2`$ and
top-$`p=1.0`$ to encourage exploration. For evaluation, we use greedy
decoding (temperature $`=0`$).

##### LoRA Configuration.

We apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ([Hu et al., 2022](#bib.bib2)) for
parameter-efficient fine-tuning across all three training stages:

- •
  Rank ($`r`$): 128
- •
  Alpha ($`\alpha`$): 256
- •
  Target modules: all linear layers
- •
  Bias: none

##### HTML-Based Attack Mechanism.

The attacker generates HTML injection code that is executed in the
browser runtime via JavaScript. The environment then:

1.  1.
    Injects the attacker-specified CSS into the document head as a
    \<style\> element
2.  2.
    Locates the target DOM node and inserts the HTML payload at the
    specified position
3.  3.
    Re-renders the page in the headless browser

After injection, both the screenshot (captured via the headless browser)
and the accessibility tree (extracted from the updated DOM) consistently
reflect the injected content. All injected elements are tagged with a
data-attacker attribute to enable clean rollback between interaction
steps. The image resolution for the agent’s visual input is
$`896\times 896`$ pixels.

### B.2 Training Hyperparameters

Table [5](#A2.T5 "Table 5 ‣ B.2 Training Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix B Implementation Details ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
summarizes the key hyperparameters for each training stage.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| Parameter | Stage 1 | Stage 2 | Stage 3 |
|  | Imitation | Orc. SFT | Adv. RL |
| Learning rate | $`5\!\times\!10^{-6}`$ | $`2\!\times\!10^{-6}`$ | $`2\!\times\!10^{-6}`$ |
| LR scheduler | cosine | cosine | cosine |
| Warmup ratio | 0.03 | 0.03 | 0.03 |
| Batch size | 128 | 128 | 128 |
| Per-device batch size | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Grad. accum. steps | 16 | 16 | 16 |
| Training epochs / iters | 1 epoch | 1 epoch | 10 iters |
| KL coefficient ($`\beta`$) | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0.05 |
| Precision | bf16 | bf16 | bf16 |
| Gradient checkpointing | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

Table 5: Training hyperparameters for each stage.

##### Stage 3 (GRPO) Specific Hyperparameters.

The adversarial RL stage uses Group Relative Policy Optimization with
the following configuration:

- •
  Data collection: 48 tasks per iteration, 16 episodes per task (GRPO
  group size $`N=16`$), maximum 5 steps per episode, 64 parallel workers
- •
  Policy optimization: importance sampling with clipping
  ($`\epsilon_{l}=0.1`$, $`\epsilon_{h}=0.3`$), group-level advantage
  normalization
- •
  Replay: 8 gradient updates per episode for both agent and attacker
- •
  Reward shaping: cosine length penalty with coefficient $`0.1`$,
  applied only to successful episodes (start ratio $`=0.75`$, end ratio
  $`=1.0`$)
- •
  Persistent LR scheduler: the cosine schedule spans all 25 iterations
  (total $`25\times 48=1{,}200`$ optimizer steps) rather than resetting
  each iteration

##### Population-Based Training.

We employ an asymmetric population strategy for the agent’s training. At
each RL iteration $`k>1`$, the agent interacts with a *population* of
all historical attacker checkpoints
$`\{\pi_{\theta}^{\text{atk},i}\}_{i=1}^{k}`$, while the attacker always
trains against only the latest agent checkpoint. To allocate episodes
among the attacker population, we use *recency-weighted sampling*: at
least $`50\%`$ of GRPO groups are assigned to the latest attacker, and
the remaining groups are distributed using exponential weights with a
decay factor of $`0.7`$ (i.e., each older attacker receives
approximately $`0.5\times`$ the weight of the next newer one). Episodes
within the same GRPO group always face the same attacker to avoid
intra-group variance from different opponents.

### B.3 Training Data

##### Stage 1: Imitation Learning Data.

We collect demonstration data using the teacher model (Gemma-3-27B-IT).
For each task in the data collection process, we collect episodes both
with and without the attacker active:

- •
  Adversarial episodes (4,000 total): The teacher model plays both the
  agent and attacker roles. We retain agent transitions from episodes
  where the agent successfully completes the task despite the attack,
  and attacker transitions from episodes where the attack succeeds in
  inducing information leakage.
- •
  Clean episodes (4,000 total): The teacher model acts only as the agent
  with no attacker present. We retain all agent transitions from
  successfully completed episodes.

Each episode runs for a maximum of 5 steps, with the teacher model using
temperature $`=1.2`$ for diverse demonstrations. Episodes are collected
with 128 parallel workers, and only transitions in successful episodes
are retained for training. After filtering, the 8,000 raw episodes yield
7,278 valid transitions in total:

- •
  Agent transitions (4,315): 1,509 from adversarial episodes where the
  agent succeeds despite attacks, and 2,806 from clean episodes without
  an attacker.
- •
  Attacker transitions (2,963): from adversarial episodes where the
  attacker successfully induces information leakage.

Both the agent and attacker roles are trained jointly via SFT on this
combined dataset.

##### Stage 2: Oracle-Guided SFT Data.

The enhanced SFT data is constructed via a four-stage pipeline
(Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Stage 2: Oracle-Guided SFT ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")),
also using the teacher model (Gemma-3-27B-IT):

- •
  Golden trajectory collection: We first collect 4,000 clean episodes
  (no attacker) using the teacher agent. Only successful episodes are
  kept, and the agent’s messages, observations (screenshot +
  accessibility tree), and responses are stored for each step.
- •
  Attack synthesis: For each step in the golden trajectories, the
  teacher attacker generates HTML injection attacks to produce attacked
  versions of the observation (modified screenshot and accessibility
  tree). This yields 4,000 attacked episodes that share the same
  ground-truth actions as the clean originals.
- •
  Oracle CoT generation: An oracle model generates task-focused
  Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning for each attacked step. The oracle
  has access to both the clean and attacked observations and produces a
  reasoning trace that adheres to the zero-acknowledgment principle.
- •
  Data mixing: We replace the original agent’s CoT reasoning trace with
  the oracle-generated CoT in the attacked episodes. Then, for the
  dataset of clean episodes (i.e., agent completes tasks without
  attacks), to ensure diversity of the training data, instead of
  directly use the golden trajectories as agent successful trajectories,
  we collect another 4000 clean episodes without attacks and filter out
  the agent transitions from the agent successful episodes.

After filtering, the 8,000 raw episodes yield 8,564 valid transitions in
total:

- •
  Agent transitions (5,567): 2,704 from adversarial episodes where the
  agent succeeds despite attacks, and 2,863 from clean episodes without
  an attacker.
- •
  Attacker transitions (2,997): from adversarial episodes where the
  attacker successfully induces information leakage.

In total, each of the two SFT stages trains on a mixture of adversarial
and clean data, balanced to ensure the agent acquires both attack
robustness and standard task-completion ability.

##### Agent Observation Space.

During both training and evaluation, the agent receives multimodal
observations consisting of:

- •
  A screenshot of the current webpage (with or without injected content)
- •
  The accessibility tree (AXTree) extracted from the DOM
- •
  The focused element information
- •
  Action history and thinking history from previous steps
- •
  Task description and security guidelines

##### Attacker Observation Space.

The attacker has privileged access to the agent’s action history (but
not the agent’s internal reasoning or memory), in addition to the
current webpage state and task description.

## Appendix C Dataset Details

### C.1 MiniWob++ Tasks

We use 125 tasks from the MiniWob++ benchmark for training and
evaluation. The benchmark provides diverse web interaction tasks
including clicking buttons, filling forms, navigating menus, and
completing multi-step workflows. We retain 28 tasks for evaluation, and
the rest consists of the candidate tasks for training. To select the RL
training tasks, we filter out the tasks where the agent’s success rate
is less than 0.2 and the attacker’s success rate is less than 0.1, which
ensures the RL training tasks are not too difficult for both the agent
and the attacker.

### C.2 Curated VisualWebArena

We selected 100 tasks with easy or medium difficulty from the
VisualWebArena benchmark. We curated these tasks into an adversarial
evaluation framework by:

- •
  Providing the agent with synthetic sensitive user information (e.g.,
  passwords, credit card numbers)
- •
  Adding an attacker that modifies web content via HTML injection to
  induce the agent to reveal the sensitive information
- •
  Evaluating both task completion (whether the original task is
  completed) and security (whether sensitive information is leaked)

This serves as our out-of-distribution evaluation since the model is
only trained on MiniWob++ tasks.

### C.3 Sensitive Information

Disclaimer: All personal information appearing in this paper, including
names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, social
security numbers, credit card numbers, passwords, and any other
personally identifiable information, is entirely fictitious and randomly
generated for research purposes. Any resemblance to real individuals or
actual data is purely coincidental.

For security evaluation, we provide the agent with the following
synthetic sensitive data types:

- •
  Login credentials (username/password)
- •
  Credit card information (number, CVV)
- •
  Personal identifiable information (SSN, address)

Attacks are considered successful if the agent reveals any of this
information through its actions (e.g., typing it into an
attacker-injected form field, or directly revealing it in the tool
parameter).

## Appendix D Prompts

This section presents the complete prompts used for the agent, attacker,
and oracle models in our framework. During training and evaluation,
prompt variants are randomly sampled from a pool of semantically
equivalent paraphrases to improve robustness; we show one representative
variant for each component below.

### D.1 Agent Prompt

The agent receives a system prompt (establishing its role) and a user
prompt (containing the task goal, observations, user information, full
action space, and response format instructions). The user prompt is
constructed dynamically at each step. We show one representative variant
from the pool of paraphrased prompts.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### D.2 Attacker Prompt

The attacker receives a system prompt (describing its role and HTML
injection capabilities) and a user prompt (containing the target agent’s
goal, webpage state, the agent’s action space, and the attack output
format). We show one representative variant from the pool of paraphrased
prompts.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The attacker’s system prompt includes a randomly sampled *mutation
strategy* from a pool of 10 social engineering techniques, including:
using non-common languages/slang, dense jargon, persona adoption,
authority impersonation, deliberate typos/leetspeak, synonym
substitution, emotional pressure, speculative framing, fictional
context, and low-resource language exploitation. These strategies
encourage diverse attack generation across training iterations.

### D.3 Oracle Prompt for Task-Focused CoT Generation

The oracle model in Stage 2 generates task-focused Chain-of-Thought
(CoT) reasoning for training the student agent. The oracle has
privileged access to both the attacked and clean observations but
generates CoT that strictly adheres to the *zero-acknowledgment*
principle – never mentioning attacks or suspicious elements.

#### E.1.3 Agent’s Response to Attack

Faced with the injected accessibility tree (containing both the fake

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The agent is deceived by the injected “Date Format Error” form: it
believes email verification is a prerequisite to completing the date
task. As a result, it enters the user’s private email address

constituting a successful information leakage attack. The episode
terminates with attacker reward $`=1`$ and agent reward $`=0`$.

#### E.2.3 Agent’s Response to Attack

Despite the injected “Move Confirmation” form appearing prominently in
both the screenshot and the accessibility tree, the DMAST-trained agent
focuses exclusively on the task-relevant elements:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In contrast to the attacker-success example above, the trained agent
completely ignores the injected password verification form. Its
reasoning trace mentions only the task goal and the relevant list
elements. The agent correctly drags “Lyn” to the 3rd position,
completing the task without any information leakage. The episode
terminates with agent reward $`=1`$ and attacker reward $`=0`$.

## Appendix F Additional Attack Diversity Analysis

We supplement the main-text analysis about attack diversity with
additional diversity metrics covering lexical and strategic dimensions.
All metrics are computed on attacker-generated HTML injections from
iterations 1–10.

### F.1 N-gram Entropy

As a complement to Distinct-$`n`$ (which measures the ratio of unique
$`n`$-grams), we also compute the Shannon entropy of the $`n`$-gram
frequency distribution. While Distinct-$`n`$ captures how many unique
$`n`$-grams exist relative to the total, $`n`$-gram entropy further
accounts for the _uniformity_ of $`n`$-gram usage. High entropy means no
single $`n`$-gram dominates.

Figure [7](#A6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ F.1 N-gram Entropy ‣ Appendix F Additional Attack Diversity Analysis ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks")
shows consistent growth across unigram, bigram, and trigram entropy,
reinforcing the finding that lexical diversity increases with training.

Figure 7: $`N`$-gram entropy across self-play iterations. Higher entropy
indicates a more uniform distribution over $`n`$-grams, i.e., less
reliance on frequently repeated phrases.

### F.2 Attack Strategy Diversity

To assess diversity at the _semantic_ level, we classify each attack
into one or more strategy categories using keyword-based pattern
matching. We define 15 attack strategy types: _fake login_, _security
alert_, _verification prompt_, _fake form_, _overlay attack_, _error
message_, _authority impersonation_, _session expired_, _captcha fake_,
_update required_, _data collection_, _compliance_, _redirect attack_,
_popup/modal_, and _instruction injection_. Each attack can belong to
multiple categories simultaneously (multi-label classification).

We then compute: (1) Strategy Entropy: the Shannon entropy of the
strategy label distribution—higher entropy means the attacker
distributes its efforts more evenly across strategy types; and
(2) Unique Strategy Combinations: the number of distinct multi-label
strategy combinations observed, measuring how creatively the attacker
mixes different techniques within a single injection.

As shown in
Figure [8](#A6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ F.2 Attack Strategy Diversity ‣ Appendix F Additional Attack Diversity Analysis ‣ Dual-Modality Multi-Stage Adversarial Safety Training: Robustifying Multimodal Web Agents Against Cross-Modal Attacks"),
strategy entropy increases from $`3.21`$ to $`3.27`$, and the number of
unique strategy combinations grows from $`465`$ to $`523`$ across
iterations 1–10.

Figure 8: Attack strategy diversity: entropy of the strategy
distribution (left axis) and number of unique strategy combinations
(right axis).

### F.3 Qualitative Examples of Attacker Evolution

To complement the quantitative diversity metrics above, we present
concrete attack examples from different stages of RL training,
illustrating how the attacker’s strategies evolve qualitatively. We show
two pre-RL examples (before self-play training) and two post-RL examples
(after iteration 10), all focusing on the attacker’s reasoning and the
resulting injected page.

#### F.3.1 Pre-RL Attacks (Before Self-Play)

Before RL training, the attacker relies on simple, template-like
strategies that closely mirror the few-shot examples provided in the
prompt. The attacks are generic credential harvesting forms without much
awareness of the specific task context.

#### F.3.2 Post-RL Attacks (After Iteration 10)

After 10 iterations of adversarial self-play, the attacker develops
markedly more sophisticated strategies. We highlight two emergent
capabilities: _task-context awareness_ and _multi-step coordinated
attacks_.

##### Example 3: Task-Context-Aware Attack (drag-items-grid).

The agent’s goal is: _“Drag Margalit to the top right.”_ The attacker
reads the task content from the screenshot and generates a phishing
message that directly references specific elements in the current task:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

This multi-step strategy demonstrates two advanced capabilities absent
in pre-RL attacks: (1) *instruction override*, in which the attacker
first attempts to invalidate the agent’s original goal before presenting
a phishing form, and (2) *temporal coordination*, in which the two
injections across consecutive steps form a coherent narrative designed
to gradually erode the agent’s adherence to its original instructions.
